reflexion_entries_to_archive: S149 P1 — THE ROOT CAUSE WAS A DESIGN FROM THE PREVIOUS GAME, NOT A BUG. `isInsideEnemyTerritory` faithfully implemented an influence-bubble rule; it was never broken. The owner's 'players can build wherever' was the correct observation of a rule that had been superseded on paper and never in code. Look for superseded-but-still-running rules, not just defects.

S149 P1 — MY OWN TEST WAS THE WEAK LINK, AND ONLY MUTATION TESTING FOUND IT. The first draft of the agreement sweep called computePreviewBonds and then read `canBuildAt` for the verdict, so it would have passed with gate 4 completely unwired. Writing the test is not the same as the test working: break the code on purpose and confirm the test screams.

S149 P1 — 'STILL PASSES' IS NOT 'STILL TESTING WHAT IT SAYS'. placeFromFree's atomicity test stayed green through the swap but its stated cause (an enemy prim's territorial radius) had been replaced by a different one (the zone). A test that passes for a new reason is a comment that has become a lie. Documented it rather than enjoying the green.

S149 P1 — THE FALSE PASS CAME FROM MY OWN VERIFICATION, NOT THE CODE. `grep dist/assets/index-*.js | head -1` read a 3.7KB chunk instead of the 705KB entry, and reported the fixture stripped. The recorded S132 trap was about grepping dist/ recursively; this was the same trap wearing a new costume. Resolve the artifact from index.html, and always include a positive control.

S149 P1 — A COPIED COORDINATE CARRIED A HIDDEN ASSUMPTION ACROSS FILES. bomb.spec built at x=1500 with the comment 'same coords as smoke.spec.ts Sym F'. In smoke the placer is the JOINER (right half); in bomb it is SOLO (left half). The comment recorded WHERE the numbers came from but not WHAT made them valid, so the borrowing survived until the rule changed.

S149 P1 — TWO GATES CAN FAIL IDENTICALLY. Moving placeFromFree's fixtures onto legal ground made them fail the 250px avatar-REACH gate instead, with the same assertion message (primitives.size short by one). Loosening the zone rule would have 'fixed' it and hidden a real second gate. When a fix does not take, check whether a DIFFERENT gate is now the one refusing.

S149 P1 — THE PLAN SAID 'six one-line edits'. It was six edits plus 17 test repairs plus 3 e2e repairs plus a shared fixture plus 62 new assertions. The prior session measured the 17 and reverted; the e2e blast radius was never measured by anyone and only surfaced by running the lane. A measured blast radius from a revert is a FLOOR, not the total.

S149 P2 — A GREEN SUITE MEANT NOTHING. After landing four behavioural changes (shelter, build gate, dormancy, quarry) the suite reported the EXACT pre-change count: 2629, not one test touched. 163 files and not one would have noticed if the split had been wired backwards. When a change to behaviour moves no test count at all, that is the signal to write the test — not evidence the change was safe.

S149 P2 — THE FROZEN-REFERENCE GATE FIRED AND IT WAS RIGHT. All 8 differential scenarios died, but NOT on a hash divergence — on CarryViolation during FIXTURE SETUP, because the fixture pins FIGHT and then builds, which P2 had just outlawed. Reading the actual error instead of assuming 'the reference needs re-baselining' was the whole difference between an ordering fix and quietly laundering a real gate.

S149 P2 — I ASSERTED A DETERMINISM PROPERTY I COULD NOT DEMONSTRATE. My test claimed deposits land in the bank in gatherer-id order; the bank is a per-TYPE TALLY, so deposits commute and order is unobservable there. The test failing is what taught me my own docblock over-claimed. Kept the sort (cheap, forward-looking) but rewrote the justification to what is true.

S149 P2 — COMPOSE THE RULE ONCE, IMMEDIATELY. P1 spent a whole priority collapsing six copies of build legality onto one predicate. Adding `matchPhase !== BUILD` at those same six sites would have rebuilt the identical problem one priority later. `canBuildNow` composes WHERE and WHEN in one place — and the ONE gate that legitimately differs (the stamp, which owes the player a reason word) is documented as a deliberate exception rather than an oversight.

S149 P2 — GATE THE DISPATCH, NOT THE SOURCE. The obvious quarry fix was to skip `spawner.tick` during FIGHT. That would have advanced the seeded RNG stream differently on host vs the worker mirror the instant their phases disagreed for one tick. The file already documented the correct pattern for four hazards; reading the neighbouring code beat inventing a fix.

S149 P2 — A REFUSAL THAT NAMES THE WRONG REASON IS A BUG. Routing the stamp through the shared predicate would have told a player 'ENEMY GROUND' while they stood on their own territory. The panel's own standing contract is that a disabled control says why, so the phase got its own refusal word. Sharing a predicate is right; sharing it at the cost of an honest message is not.

S149 P3 — HALF THE OWNER'S COMPLAINT WAS A RENDER DEFECT AND I ALMOST MISSED IT. 'There are no walls it seems or player zones' — P1 answered the mechanics and I nearly moved on. Probing for P3 found that NOTHING drew the partition at all, so players were refused on ground they could not see they did not own. When a complaint has two clauses, check whether they have two different causes.

S149 P3 — I WIRED A FEATURE AND A TEST PROVED IT WAS THE WRONG FEATURE. Wiring the wall clamp into gatherer movement dropped the opening economy below a first tower, because rim-snapped sparks belong to neighbouring zones. Following that through showed border walls have NO blocking role at all — the sealing comes from build legality and dormancy. The right response was to revert the wiring and write down WHY, not to special-case the rim until the test went green.

S149 P3 — A TESTED FUNCTION WITH NO CALLER IS NOT A FEATURE. `clampAcrossWalls` had eight passing tests and zero consumers, which reads as done and is not. Checking 'who actually calls this?' before closing is what turned a silent gap into a documented carry-forward.

S149 P3 — THE ROLL-CALL ASSERTION PAID FOR ITSELF. fog.spec names every child of aboveFogLayer in order specifically so an added renderer points at the index that moved; adding the wall renderer failed it instantly and legibly. A bare `length === 16` would have said 'expected 16, received 17' and cost a session, which is exactly why a previous session rewrote it.

S149 P3 — ONE FAILURE IN A LANE IS NOT A FLAKE UNTIL MEASURED. rainbow.spec failed once. Rather than assert flake, I ran it 3x isolated (3/3, runtimes 16.6-35.9s showing real load variance) and re-ran the full lane clean. The evidence supported intermittence; asserting it without the runs would have been the exact mistake the standing lesson warns about.

S149 P3 — PIN THE AWKWARD CONSEQUENCE INSTEAD OF HIDING IT. Walls stopping at the quarry rim means a unit can route between zones through the centre. That looks like a hole, and it follows directly from the owner's own Q6 access rule. A named test plus a carry-forward turns 'a bug someone finds in playtest' into 'a design question with the owner's name on it'.

S149 P4 — A PROSE WARNING NAMED A SOLUTION, NOT THE REQUIREMENT. zones.test.ts said 'if a footer is ever revived, these anchors move up'. The actual invariant was 'no chip may overlap a porch', which centring the bar satisfies without touching two shipped anchors. Read an inherited warning for the CONSTRAINT it protects, not the fix it happens to suggest — then convert it to an assertion so the next session inherits a test instead of a sentence.

S149 P4 — THE SCREENSHOT FOUND WHAT 166 GREEN FILES COULD NOT. Unaffordable chips were rendered in a tint that was invisible against the board, so the bar existed and communicated nothing. No unit test can assert legibility. For any UI surface, LOOK at it before calling it done.

S149 P4 — I MISCOUNTED MY OWN UI FROM A SCREENSHOT. At 1280x720 a 62px chip is 41px, and I read three where there were five. A photograph is evidence that something rendered; it is not a measurement. Exposing the geometry and asserting it turned a guess into a permanent guard.

S149 P4 — WHEN A GUARDRAIL BLOCKS A CLEANUP COMMAND, CHANGE THE COMMAND. The destructive guard refused `rm -rf` on a scratch dir. The right response was a non-recursive delete, not an override token — the guard was doing exactly its job on a pattern that is usually catastrophic.

S149 P5 — MY DEFERRAL SHIPPED SOMETHING THAT LOOKED BROKEN. I logged the footer's tower menu as CF-S149-c and shipped chips that toggled a selection and opened nothing. The owner read that as 'it isnt clickable' — correctly. A half-built AFFORDANCE is worse than none: it advertises a capability and then does nothing. Defer whole features, never the visible half of one.

S149 P5 — I SHIPPED WALLS ONTO THE TITLE SCREEN AND ONLY A SCREENSHOT FOUND IT. `wallsAreUp` asks about matchPhase, and a world that has never started a match still reads BUILD. Every test passed. Any renderer keyed on a phase/mode field needs the gameState guard too, and the only way I found it was looking at an unrelated capture.

S149 P5 — Z-ORDER IS DECIDED BY CONSTRUCTION ORDER, AND CONSTRUCTION ORDER IS DECIDED BY DEPENDENCIES. Both the footer (under the fog) and the arcade menu (under the title) were built before the thing that had to sit beneath them. Re-parenting at show/init time is the fix that does not fight the dependency graph.

S149 P5 — WHEN THE OWNER MOVES A SURFACE, MOVE THE STATE'S UI, NOT THE STATE. The build grid moved from castle to footer, but `armed` stayed on the castle panel because controls.ts, the cursor ghost and the commit path all read it. One new `armExternal` entry point inherited every downstream behaviour; re-homing the state would have meant rewiring the whole carry flow to chase a UI decision.

S149 P6 — DELEGATION WORKED BECAUSE THE BRIEFS CARRIED THE TRAPS. Both agents were handed the measured cost structure (nine sites for a hashed World field, five for a protocol bump), the determinism rules, and the mixed-line-endings hazard. Both came back with mutation-verified work and correct protocol bumps. A brief that only states the GOAL gets a plausible answer; one that states the goal plus the known ways to get it wrong gets a correct one.

S149 P6 — TWO AGENTS ON ONE TREE COST ME REAL TIME. One left a TEMP probe that duplicated an object key and broke tsc for everyone; the other correctly reported the tree was dirty and that 57 type errors were not theirs. Next time: give each agent a disjoint file set explicitly, or run them sequentially when they both touch main.ts.

S149 P6 — 'STALE' AND 'FLAKY' ARE NOT THE SAME WORD. click-to-build broke because the surface it drives MOVED. Tagging it @quarantine-flaky would have been the convenient lie and would have buried a real regression later. test.fixme plus the rewrite recipe keeps the gate green AND keeps the debt visible.

S149 P6 — I SHIPPED THE SAME CLASS OF BUG TWICE IN ONE SESSION. Border walls drew on the title screen because a never-started world reads matchPhase BUILD; the HUD agent then found FOUR MORE instruments leaking onto the title for the identical reason (world.players holds P1 from boot, so every 'is the player alive' guard passes on the menu). Any renderer keyed on a phase or roster field needs the gameState guard too — that is now a rule, not an observation.

#a-human-checks-the-last-link-a-machine-checks-every-link - I set out to repair two known gaps in the protocol changelog and found four, because I wrote a completeness check instead of reading the block. 8->9 had been missing since S93 and 20->21 since S144 - eight and three bumps, through multiple sessions that each read that comment and pronounced it complete, including two whose whole purpose was fixing this drift. The reason is structural: when a human validates a chain they check that the LAST entry matches the constant, because that is the cheap end-to-end check, and interior links are invisible to that method no matter how carefully you read. So the lesson is not 'read more carefully' - it is that any invariant of the form 'this sequence is complete' should be enumerated by code the first time you touch it, and the cost is fifteen lines.

#my-first-gate-was-wrong-and-the-failure-was-the-most-useful-output - The chain test's first draft asserted both changelog carriers run from version 2, and it went red on the HelloMsg list for 2-6. My instinct was that I had found a sixth drift instance. I had not: that list was simply started later, at 6->7, and the FILE was right while my TEST was wrong. Had I 'fixed' the file to satisfy my gate I would have fabricated four changelog entries for bumps I know nothing about - the exact failure mode I had just finished refuting in two external reviewers. The design that came out of the failure is better than my first: measure each carrier's own floor, assert no gaps above it, pin the floors separately so deletions off the front still fail. When a new gate goes red, the first hypothesis to test is that the gate is wrong.

#i-proved-the-gate-by-breaking-the-file-back - After repairing the drift I could have shipped a green test and called CF-S147-b closed. Green proves nothing about a gate: my assertions might have matched anything, or nothing. So I restored `git show HEAD:src/net/protocol.ts` over the working copy and ran the new block against the drifted file - it failed on exactly the three real classes and named the missing links [9, 21, 26, 27] out loud - then restored the repair and re-ran to 10/10. That round trip costs two commands and converts 'I wrote a test' into 'I watched this catch the specific bug it exists for'.

#the-stubbed-test-was-green-and-the-real-browser-found-the-bug-in-one-frame - Nine unit tests passed against a Pixi stub and told me the overlay was correct. Then I drove the same three screens against real Pixi in the dev server, read back what was actually drawn, and immediately saw a board with two rows both reading 0:07.25 and the highlight on the wrong one. No stub could have shown me that, because the stub had no reason to produce a colliding board - I had written the fixtures, so my fixtures had my blind spot in them. The general lesson is not 'stubs are bad': it is that a stub tests the logic I thought of, and a live surface tests the DATA the system actually produces. When something renders, look at what it rendered.

#i-could-not-screenshot-so-i-said-so-instead-of-implying-i-had - The browser pane cannot composite in this session and Pixi refuses synthetic pointer events, so two things I would normally verify - contrast and z-order - were genuinely unverifiable. The temptation was to let 'runtime-verified in a real browser' stand and leave the gap implied, since it is true and sounds complete. I wrote the limit into check_method explicitly instead, because this repo's recorded traps are exactly the visual ones and a future session reading 'runtime-verified' would reasonably assume the frame had been looked at. Verification claims should name their axis.

#the-fourth-fixme-was-not-a-stale-test-and-i-had-written-it-up-as-one - My own PDR listed 'FOUR test.fixme, not three' as a finding and lumped all four together as stale surfaces. Reading the fourth one's BODY instead of its title changed the classification completely: it hardcodes `return null` and then asserts `not.toBeNull()`, so it has never been capable of passing, and it checks a '/50' readout from an era when the win score was 50 rather than 1500. Three stale tests and one placeholder are different problems with different fixes - the stale ones needed a new surface, the placeholder needs instrumentation that does not exist. The habit worth keeping: a `fixme` inventory built from grep gives you titles, and titles are the least reliable part of a test. Open the body before you size the work.

#two-wrong-hypotheses-then-the-data-and-the-order-mattered - I spent this priority being wrong twice. The file's own comment blamed the AttractDrag; a probe showed the spark lands 0-2 px from the cursor, six times out of six. I then blamed the S149 phase boundary, proved placements really are refused after tick 5400, shipped a guard for it - and the guard never fired, because the real failures were at tick 2900. Only when I stopped proposing causes and instead made the FAILURE MESSAGE carry state did the answer appear in one line: rainbows=1. The lesson is about sequencing rather than humility: with an intermittent bug the cheapest first move is not a hypothesis, it is instrumenting the failure so the next occurrence indicts itself. I had the tooling to do that in five minutes and I did it fourth.

#a-partial-fix-looked-exactly-like-no-fix-and-nearly-cost-me-the-real-one - Suppressing bombs took the failure rate from 2/6 to 3/8. Read naively that is 'no change, revert it' - and reverting would have been wrong, because bombs WERE genuinely stealing the mouse-down in the two failures I had measured. Two independent causes produced one symptom, and fixing one moved the rate by less than the noise in an n=8 sample. What saved it was the diagnostic printing bombs=0 on the NEXT failures: not a rate, but a direct statement that the first cause was gone and something else remained. When causes are independent and each is sufficient, pass rates cannot tell you whether a fix worked - only per-failure evidence can.

#the-denominator-is-the-claim - Every number here is quoted with its trial count: 2/6 before, 3/8 after the partial, 0/8 after the full fix, and the lane 49/1/3 -> 53/0/0. That came from a prior session's note that 'flaky is a diagnosis that needs a denominator', and it earned its keep twice: it told me the bomb fix had NOT resolved things when the phrase 'fixed the bomb race' would have implied it had, and it is the only reason '0 fail' means anything now.

#normalising-on-write-without-normalising-on-read-is-a-two-line-bug-in-one-commit - My P3 fix made recordRun store normaliseName(name) so a blank row could never reach the board. The overlay's highlight kept matching on the RAW initials, so a player who spelled three spaces had 'AAA' stored and '   ' searched for, and their own row silently stopped lighting up. Both halves were in the same commit and I wrote both. The shape to watch for is not 'normalisation is risky' - it is that adding a transform to a WRITE path creates an obligation on every READ path that matches on the written value, and nothing in the type system or the tests represents that obligation. The audit found it in one pass by asking what five keystrokes could produce.

#a-one-constant-edit-crossed-the-wire-and-the-diff-gave-no-hint - VOLTKIN_HP 2 to 8 looked like a balance dial. It owed a protocol bump, because serializeCreature omits creature hp when the creature is UNDAMAGED - so an undamaged Voltkin carries no hp at all and the peer rebuilds it from its own compiled constant. An optimisation made in a different session for unrelated reasons (save bytes on the common case) had quietly turned that constant into shared state. The general rule, now written into the changelog with its three instances named: an additive-optional field whose ABSENCE means 'use your own default' makes that default a shared constant both peers compute from. Omitting a field to save bytes does not make its value private. The satisfying part is that P1's gate, built four priorities earlier in the same session, is what made the six-site bump mechanical instead of another drift instance.

reflexion_entries_to_archive.title: Archiving a feature is worth more than the copy — the value is the excision checklist
reflexion_entries_to_archive.what_happened: Owner R73 asked for the four hazard families archived whole. The copy itself was 20 minutes of work. What actually mattered was the 10-point EXCISION CHECKLIST in RESTORE.md, because A.0 showed the hazard-OWNED files (26) are the small half: the real cost is the hazard-shaped holes in SHARED files — 5 World Maps, 5 NetSnapshot arrays, 5 hashed unions, 16 action types of which 4 are client intents, 5 id brands, an RNG-neutrality invariant, and poop's separate debuff reach into placeFromFree.
lessons: ⭐ ENUMERATE BY FILENAME, NOT BY IMPORT-READING. `find -iname` caught src/render/effects/bombExplode.ts, which does not sit beside the other bomb files. Reading the import graph by eye would have shipped a 25-file archive that LOOKED complete. This is the S150 'enumerate a chain, do not read it' trap in a new costume.

⭐ PROVE INERTNESS ACROSS EVERY RUNNER SEPARATELY. A copied test tree is only harmless if tsc, vitest AND playwright each ignore it. Three configs, three independent checks (include=['src'], test.include=['src/**/*.test.ts'], testDir='./e2e'). Checking one and assuming the others is how a duplicated spec suite starts failing in a lane nobody was watching.

⭐ AN UNCHANGED BUILD HASH IS POSITIVE EVIDENCE, not just a null result. index-CPfPN4k_.js identical before and after proves no src/ drift more strongly than `git status`, because it is derived from the actual compiled output rather than from what git happened to notice.

⭐ QUOTE THE DENOMINATOR (S150 trap, applied prospectively). 44 gating + 9 archived = 53 = the original count. Without that arithmetic, 'the lane is green now' is indistinguishable from 'I deleted the failing tests'.

⛔ NEVER READ A TEST RUNNER'S EXIT CODE THROUGH A PIPE. `npm run e2e:gating | tail` printed 'exited with code 0' while Playwright had 1 failure — the pipeline returns tail's status. This nearly let a red lane read as green during preflight, and it is now recorded in the PDR and the commit message.

⛔ DO NOT LEAVE EXPLORATORY COMMANDS IN A MUTATING CHAIN. A stray speculative sed corrupted package.json to 'XXX'. It was caught only because I read the result back instead of trusting the command's silence. Mutation and exploration should never share a shell invocation.

A carry-forward's PREDICTED CAUSE deserves the same distrust as any other unverified claim. CF-S150-b named the flyover cinematic; the instrument S150 itself added reports lockedByCinematic:FALSE in both failures. The prediction was recorded confidently and was wrong — so the archive records the EVIDENCE and marks the new hypothesis explicitly unconfirmed, rather than replacing one confident guess with another.

reflexion_entries_to_archive.title: The compiler found the structure; the compiler could NOT find the semantics
reflexion_entries_to_archive.what_happened: Deleted five accidental backbones and put units, towers and connectors on one shared stat ladder in exact-integer fifths. Protocol 28->29 for four simultaneous wire breaks. The owner supplied the full stat table mid-priority (R77), which RECLASSIFIED Helga from tower to unit and invalidated part of what I had just built.
lessons: ⭐ A TYPE CHANGE IS TSC-FORCED; A UNIT CHANGE IS NOT. Renaming Creature.hp -> ehp turned every unconverted site into a compile error. But the sites that PASS a number — attackFifths vs a raw 1 — compile clean and silently deal one fifth of the intended damage. Those had to be enumerated by hand. When a quantity's MEANING changes, rename it; the rename is the only mechanism that recruits the compiler.

⛔ MY OWN AUTOMATION WROTE THE WORST BUG OF THE PRIORITY. A patch script inserted a hardcoded `damageFifths: 0` into a PRODUCTION deserializer. It compiled, passed 2891 tests, and would have healed every damaged connector on every snapshot apply and host migration. Green tests did not see it because no fixture damages a bond. AUDIT THE DIFF OF ANYTHING A SCRIPT TOUCHED — the blast radius of a regex is not the set of files you intended.

⛔ A SYNTACTICALLY VALID INSERTION CAN BE SEMANTICALLY DEAD. `damageFifths: 0,` placed after a single-line literal's closing brace parses as a LABEL plus a comma-expression. Two files did this and tsc was silent. Verifying 'the script said clean' is not verifying; I re-ran tsc directly and found 12 more errors my own regex had missed.

⭐ THE OWNER'S ARITHMETIC WAS AN INDEPENDENT ORACLE. R77 said the chewer is '1x1.4 offence, and 1 def'. The fifths model, built days before that sentence, produces exactly 1.4 and 1.0. That agreement is worth more than any test I could write, because it was derived from the other end.

⭐ WHEN A RULING SUPERSEDES A TEST, THE TEST SHOULD RECORD THE SUPERSESSION. 'HELGA fells a goblin in two slaps' and 'a Voltkin takes three slaps' both became false via owner rulings. Deleting them would erase the reasoning; each was replaced with the NEW invariant plus the sentence that moved it. A test suite is also a ledger of decisions.

⭐ TWO RULINGS CAN BOTH HOLD IF THEY ACT ON DIFFERENT STATS. R70 said the goblin should be 'as weak as chewer'; R77 then gave it 2 DEF. Before a stat SYSTEM existed those would have been a contradiction — one number per unit. Now R70 set its HP and R77 set its DEF and both are true. That is the clearest argument for the whole priority.

⚠ FLAG INVERSIONS, DO NOT ABSORB THEM. R77's numbers make Helga out-hit the laser, reversing the property S148 built a whole test file to protect. It is defensible, it is the owner's call, and it is now stated in code, in the PDR and to the owner — rather than quietly encoded.

reflexion_entries_to_archive.what_happened: Shipped the goblin tower — one tower, six outputs — plus animated art for the melee goblin, the archer and the stink tower, built from the owner's own designs. Protocol 29->30. Everything typechecked and 2924 tests passed while THREE separate open pathways sat in the tree.
lessons: ⭐ THE BIGGEST DEFECTS OF THIS PRIORITY HAD NO FAILING TEST. The tower was IMMORTAL (no recipeStillSatisfied case, so its default arm kept it alive off one lone Circle), UNBUILDABLE (ALL_BLUEPRINT_IDS is a hand-written array that tsc does not exhaustiveness-check, unlike the Record two lines above it), and its panel row had NO COPY. All green. All invisible. Deliberately asking 'can a player actually REACH this?' is a different act from running the suite.

⛔ I COMMITTED A TRAP THIS REPO DOCUMENTS IN CAPITALS. blueprints.ts says do not value-import a recipe module from anything world.ts reaches, because registerRecipe fires at the tail. I did it anyway, and the symptom was a ?worker=1 bots match never leaving TITLE — pointing nowhere near the import. Reading a warning is not the same as recognising your own code as the thing it warns about. The structural fix (a side-effect-free leaf) beats remembering the rule.

⚠ I OVERCLAIMED CAUSATION AND HAD TO CORRECT MYSELF. I wrote 'CONFIRMS the cause' into a commit message on the strength of ONE passing re-run, in a repo that had already burned a session on a 50%-flaky spec. Re-ran 3/3 before letting it stand. One green run after a fix is a hypothesis, not a confirmation — the same discipline I applied to the rainbow flake, forgotten when the result was the one I wanted.

⭐ AN EXHAUSTIVE Record IS A DESIGN INSTRUMENT, NOT A TYPE ANNOTATION. Adding five creature types produced five separate failures, each forcing a decision the owner would otherwise never have been asked: what is this unit FOR, what may it hit, what does it cost to bench it. That is exactly what the owner asked for — 'needs to be within our build as a natural law of things' — and it is now enforced by the compiler rather than by discipline.

⭐ VERIFY GENERATED ART BY LOOKING AT IT, ON THE WRONG BACKGROUND. Compositing each atlas on mid-grey is what exposed both matte defects: a white blob between the goblin's legs (enclosed white that border-connectivity correctly preserved and should not have) and black letterbox bars leaking in on frames where an effect filled the screen. Neither is visible on white, and no test would ever have caught either.

⭐ WHEN A PIPELINE WILL RUN AGAIN, MAKE IT A SCRIPT THE FIRST TIME. Four more goblins and the poop bags are next session. A hand-tuned crop and anchor done twice guarantees the second character floats against the first — so build-sprite-atlas.mjs carries the union-bbox and foot-anchor rules that keep a roster coherent.

⚠ DEPLOYING HALF OF A TWO-PART WIRE CHANGE COSTS A WHOLE EXTRA PROTOCOL BUMP. The PDR correctly planned P2+P3 to share 28->29. I deployed P2 first, so v29 went live without the goblin types and P3 needed 29->30. A sequencing mistake, not a design one, and cheap only because it was noticed rather than papered over.

R72.owner: the unit balance ... is all very stupidly made. a goblins power should not be the backbone for the whole stat system - there should be a system in place that we define. we will have HP STR DEF PENETRATION and other stats we can think about and define their specs. then based on that we will decide for every tower and every unit what they have. for example Helga only attacks enemy units, chewers only attack towers, goblins of all kinds can do both, laser torretr does both, lightning drones can do both, voltkin can do both. and then the stats come into play. so for example voltkin with 1HP + 1DEF = 1 ATK + 1 PEN. literally for now we will consider defence and hp as the exact inverse stat for ATK and PEN. where hp = 1 point. attack = -1 hp point (so if you attack someone and you have 1 atk and he has 1 hp thenm it only takes one attack to kill him). and DEF and PEN are multiples so def = x1.2 and pen = /1.2 . so if an enemy has 2 hp and one def. his total defensive stat is 2.4 . if he has 2 hp and 2 stats he will then have 2x1.4 = 2.8 defensive stats and so if a laser tower has 3 attack, then he will be destroyed with one laser hit.... something like that! makes sense??
R72.means: ⭐ THIS SUPERSEDES R65 AND R70 AND CORRECTS MY OWN FRAMING OF BOTH. I described PRINCESS_SLAP_DAMAGE_VS_CREATURE = round(GOBLIN_MELEE_HP / 2) as a CONSTRAINT to respect before touching the goblin. The owner is right that it is the DEFECT ITSELF: one unit's HP became the backbone of the whole damage scale by accident, so every other number is expressed relative to a grunt. The work is not 'retune the goblin carefully' — it is DELETE THE DERIVATION and give every unit and tower explicit stats from one shared system.

stat_model.stats: HP, STR (attack), DEF, PENETRATION — plus others still to be defined.
stat_model.symmetry: Defence and HP are the exact INVERSE of ATK and PEN, on ONE shared scale. The owner's example: a voltkin with 1 HP + 1 DEF is mirrored by 1 ATK + 1 PEN. So a unit's defensive rating and offensive rating are computed the same way and compared directly.
stat_model.additive_terms: HP = 1 point each. ATK = -1 HP point (1 ATK against 1 HP is a one-hit kill).
stat_model.multiplier_terms: DEF and PEN are MULTIPLIERS, and they stack LINEARLY, not compounding — this is pinned by the owner's own two examples: 2 HP + 1 DEF = 2 x 1.2 = 2.4, and 2 HP + 2 DEF = 2 x 1.4 = 2.8. Note 1.4, NOT 1.2^2 = 1.44. So the factor is (1 + 0.2 x DEF), i.e. +0.2 per point.
stat_model.worked_example: A defender with 2 HP and 2 DEF has an effective defensive rating of 2.8. A laser tower with 3 ATK exceeds it, so it dies to a single laser hit.
open_questions: ⚠ THE ONE REAL OPEN QUESTION: is ATK a THRESHOLD or a DAMAGE POOL? The owner's laser example ('destroyed with one laser hit') reads as a threshold — compare attack_eff to def_eff once, and the target either survives intact or dies. But 'attack = -1 hp point' reads as a pool, where hits accumulate. These differ enormously: under a threshold model a 2-ATK attacker can NEVER kill a 3-HP target no matter how many times it hits, and today's damageCreature is a pool. ASK.

Whether the two existing HP scales collapse into one. Creature hp is a HIT COUNT today while Primitive/defender hp is a damage pool — constants.ts names this 'the OTHER hp scale' explicitly. One shared stat system implies they merge, which is a wide change.
What the 'other stats we can think about' are. Range, attack interval and speed already exist as separate constants and may or may not join the ladder.
Whether the 1..12 ceiling is a HARD cap (validated/clamped) or just the intended design range.

ladders.HP: INTEGER POINTS, 1..12. A flat ladder with a stated ceiling of 12.
ladders.ATK: INTEGER POINTS, 1..12 — 'same for attack', i.e. the same flat ladder as HP, which is what makes them directly comparable.
ladders.DEF: MULTIPLIER LADDER: x1.2, x1.4, x1.6, x1.8, x2.0, x2.2, ... = (1 + 0.2 x DEF). LINEAR, confirmed twice over — by the owner's 2 DEF = x1.4 example and now by the explicit ladder. NOT 1.2^n.
ladders.PEN: MULTIPLIER LADDER, same shape as DEF — 'same for ... pen'. Applied as the attacker's counterpart to DEF.

stat_model.resolved_formula: ⭐ THE LADDER RESOLVES THE PEN AMBIGUITY BY MAKING IT MOOT. The two candidate readings are ALGEBRAICALLY IDENTICAL: (A) compare attack_eff = ATK x (1 + 0.2 x PEN) against def_eff = HP x (1 + 0.2 x DEF); (B) reduce the defender first — def_eff = HP x (1 + 0.2 x DEF) / (1 + 0.2 x PEN) — and compare to ATK. Since ATK >= HP x (1+0.2D)/(1+0.2P) iff ATK x (1+0.2P) >= HP x (1+0.2D), both give the same outcome for every input. So the implementation can pick whichever reads better (A is cheaper — no division, no divide-by-zero edge, and exact in integers scaled by 5) without changing behaviour. Worked check against the owner's own example: a 2 HP / 2 DEF defender is 2 x 1.4 = 2.8; a 3 ATK / 0 PEN laser is 3.0; 3.0 >= 2.8, so it dies in one hit. Matches.
